relationships.description: Connects On-Call Escalation Policies to canary deployments in the broader engineering catalog.

spark.summary: On-call escalation defines deterministic routing, acknowledgment SLAs, and tiered handoffs so production incidents reach the right responder fast without burning out engineers. Effective escalation pairs automated multi-channel paging (PagerDuty/Opsgenie) with explicit severity tiers, Incident Commander (IC) roles, and blameless post-incident feedback loops.
spark.keyTakeaway: Keep Tier-1 pages strictly actionable with a 5-minute acknowledgment timeout before escalating to a secondary, separate the Incident Commander from hands-on debuggers on SEV-1/SEV-2, and enforce a 48-hour SLA to fix or delete any noisy alert.

concept.whyItMatters: Even the most resilient architecture fails unexpectedly. Without clear escalation paths, critical outages stall in unmonitored Slack channels for 40 minutes while the wrong team guesses who owns a failing database or payment gateway—multiplying customer impact and engineer burnout.
whenToUse: Operating 24/7 production services with explicit availability SLOs (99.9%+) where delayed human intervention violates customer SLAs.
Scaling beyond a single 6-person team into multi-team microservice ownership where incidents cross network, database, and application boundaries.
Formalizing SEV-1/SEV-2 incident command, executive stakeholder updates, and customer status-page communications.
whenNotToUse: Non-urgent warnings (disk at 75%, staging test failures, dependency deprecation notices)—route these to Jira/Linear tickets or async Slack digests, never pages.
Replacing automated self-healing (Kubernetes liveness probes, autoscaling, circuit breakers) with human toil.
Paging teams for services they did not build and have no code/config authority to fix or roll back.
keyPoints: **Clear Ownership & Service Catalog**: Every alert must map to a single owning team in Backstage/PagerDuty with a runbook URL; unowned alerts are a production bug.
**Timed Multi-Layer Escalation**: Level 1 (Primary) gets 5 minutes to ACK via push/SMS/voice; on timeout, page Level 2 (Secondary), then Level 3 (Engineering Manager / Domain Lead) at 15 minutes.

**Severity-Driven Mobilization**: Define objective SEV-1 (total outage/data loss), SEV-2 (partial degradation/SLO burn), and SEV-3 (minor/workaround) criteria so responders know immediately whether to open a war room.

**Role Separation (ICS)**: On SEV-1/SEV-2, appoint an **Incident Commander (IC)** to coordinate timelines, communications, and parallel tracks while Subject Matter Experts (SMEs) focus purely on mitigation.
**Alert Hygiene & Toil Caps**: Track pages per shift; if an on-call engineer receives >2–3 non-actionable pages per week, treat alert tuning as P0 engineering work.

examples.title: Cutting Mean Time to Acknowledge (MTTA) from 22m to 3m via Tiered Escalation
examples.scenario: A fintech platform routed all alerts into a shared `#prod-alerts` Slack channel; a midnight Redis failover sat unseen for 22 minutes because engineers muted Slack overnight.
examples.outcome: Migrating critical SLO burn alerts to PagerDuty with a 5-minute push-to-phone-call escalation and automatic fallback to the Secondary + Platform Lead cut MTTA to 2.8 minutes and eliminated missed pages.

examples.title: Stopping Cross-Team Ping-Pong with IC Role & Service Graph
examples.scenario: During a SEV-1 checkout outage, Frontend blamed API Gateway, Gateway blamed Auth, and no one checked the shared RDS connection pool for 35 minutes.
examples.outcome: Introducing a mandatory SEV-1 Incident Commander (IC) rotation plus PagerDuty's service-dependency graph let the IC pull in the DB and Auth SMEs into one Zoom bridge within 4 minutes and resolve the pool exhaustion in 12 minutes.

tradeOffs.factor: Fast Escalation Timeout (3–5m) vs. Longer Window (15m)
tradeOffs.pro: A 5-minute ACK timeout ensures sleeping or commuting engineers don't delay SEV-1 recovery.
tradeOffs.con: Too short a timeout (<2m) double-pages the secondary responder while the primary is simply unlocking their phone or laptop.

tradeOffs.factor: Dedicated SRE On-Call vs. 'You Build It, You Run It'
tradeOffs.pro: Product engineers fixing their own pages feel immediate pain from flaky deploys and fix root causes 3x faster.
tradeOffs.con: Small product teams (<4 engineers) suffer severe burnout on 24/7 rotations without follow-the-sun pairing or shared platform tiers.

tradeOffs.factor: Automated War-Room Creation vs. Manual Triage
tradeOffs.pro: Tools like Incident.io or FireHydrant auto-create a Slack channel, Zoom link, Jira ticket, and status page draft in <10 seconds.
tradeOffs.con: Auto-declaring full war rooms on noisy SEV-3 alerts creates alarm fatigue; reserve auto-bridging for SEV-1/SEV-2.

failureModes.name: Alert Fatigue & Pager Desensitization
failureModes.description: High-volume, non-actionable pages (e.g., transient CPU spikes that self-recover in 90s) train engineers to blindly ACK pages and go back to sleep.
failureModes.mitigation: Delete or downgrade any alert that doesn't require immediate human action; require every page to link to a tested runbook.

failureModes.name: Single-Point-of-Failure Hero Dependency
failureModes.description: Every hard database or Kubernetes incident escalates informally to one senior staff engineer who isn't even on rotation, leading to burnout and knowledge silos.
failureModes.mitigation: Enforce shadow shifts for new engineers, document tribal knowledge in runbooks during postmortems, and rotate IC duties.

failureModes.name: Notification Pipeline Blindness
failureModes.description: An AWS region outage knocks out your self-hosted Alertmanager or Slack webhook, so nobody gets paged during the biggest outage of the year.
failureModes.mitigation: Host alerting/paging on an independent SaaS or separate region (PagerDuty, Opsgenie) and run a continuous 'dead man's switch' heartbeat check (e.g., Healthchecks.io).

failureModes.name: Missing Handoff Context Across Shifts
failureModes.description: An ongoing SEV-2 incident is handed off at 9 AM without summarizing mitigated symptoms, active feature flags, or pending rollbacks, causing the incoming shift to repeat work.
failureModes.mitigation: Mandate a structured 5-minute shift handoff template (Active Incidents, Silenced Alerts, Deployed Mitigations, Next Check-in).

commonMistakes: Creating alerts without a `runbook_url`—forcing a half-asleep engineer at 3 AM to read source code to figure out what a metric means.
Routing pages solely to Slack or email instead of phone/SMS/high-priority push notifications that bypass Do Not Disturb.
Allowing a single engineer to act as both Incident Commander and sole hands-on debugger during a multi-team SEV-1.
Skipping blameless postmortems or failing to track action items to completion, guaranteeing the same outage repeats next quarter.
Keeping a 2-person or 3-person 24/7 rotation—anything under 6–8 engineers guarantees chronic sleep deprivation and attrition.

sections.content:
## The idea

**On-call escalation** is the human-routing state machine that sits behind your monitoring stack. When an automated system cannot self-heal an SLO violation, escalation ensures the alert reaches an empowered engineer within minutes, provides immediate diagnostic context, and—if that engineer is unavailable or overwhelmed—automatically widens the circle to backups, adjacent service owners, and an Incident Commander (IC).

Good escalation optimizes two metrics simultaneously: **Mean Time to Acknowledge (MTTA)** for customers, and **sleep/cognitive load preservation** for engineers.

## Concrete walkthrough

Trace a 02:14 AM SEV-1 payment gateway degradation from alert firing to resolution:

1. **Trigger & Deduplicate (02:14)**: Prometheus/Alertmanager fires `PaymentsHighErrorBurn` (`14.4x` SLO burn) and groups 12 related pod alerts into one PagerDuty incident with `runbook_url` and Grafana dashboard links.
2. **Level 1 Page (02:14–02:19)**: PagerDuty pushes a critical alert (bypassing iOS/Android DND) to Primary On-Call A. No ACK arrives within 5 minutes.
3. **Level 2 Escalation (02:19)**: PagerDuty automatically escalates to Secondary On-Call B via SMS + voice call. B ACKs at 02:20 (`MTTA = 6m`), opens the linked runbook, and sees upstream Stripe webhook timeouts + elevated DB locks.
4. **SEV-1 Mobilization (02:23)**: B runs `/incident declare sev1` in Slack (Incident.io), auto-paging the **Incident Commander (IC)** rotation and opening `#inc-412-payments` + a Zoom bridge.
5. **Parallel Mitigation (02:25–02:38)**: The IC assigns B to roll back the 01:50 deploy while paging the Database On-Call to inspect lock contention, updating the external status page every 15 minutes until SLO burn drops to 0.

sections.eyebrow: 03 / Designing escalation policies and ICS roles
sections.content:
## Designing escalation policies and ICS roles

A resilient escalation policy separates **initial triage** from **major incident command**:

- **4-Tier Escalation Ladder**: L1 Primary (0–5m) -> L2 Secondary (5–10m) -> L3 Team Lead/EM (10–20m) -> L4 VP/On-Call Director (20m+).
- **Incident Command System (ICS) Roles**: For SEV-1/SEV-2, assign: (1) **Incident Commander** (owns decisions and coordination, never touches terminals), (2) **Operations / Tech Lead** (directs SMEs and rollbacks), and (3) **Communications Lead** (updates Statuspage and customer support).
- **Follow-the-Sun Rotations**: Split 24-hour coverage across 2–3 geographic hubs (e.g., US-West, EU, APAC) with 8–12 hour day shifts so engineers rarely wake up at 3 AM.

## Incident severity & escalation matrix

| Severity | Customer Impact Criteria | Page Urgency | Required Roles | Status Update Cadence |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **SEV-1** | Full outage, data loss, or security breach | Immediate 24/7 (5m ACK) | IC + Ops + Comms + SMEs | Every 15–30 min |
| **SEV-2** | Major feature degraded or >5% error SLO burn | Immediate 24/7 (5m ACK) | IC + Service Owner | Every 60 min |
| **SEV-3** | Minor impact with automated/manual workaround | Business hours / Slack | Single On-Call Engineer | Daily / at resolution |
| **SEV-4** | Cosmetic bug or staging failure | Ticket only (no page) | Product backlog | Normal sprint triage |

## Failure modes

**1. Escalation Loop / Dead-End Schedules**: An engineer leaves the company and their PagerDuty user is deactivated, leaving a gap in the rotation where pages drop or loop endlessly. Audit rotations automatically via CI/Terraform (`pagerduty_schedule`) synced to HR/Okta groups.

**2. Over-Escalation to Executives Too Early**: Paging VPs at minute 5 on every transient alert trains leadership to ignore pages and intimidates junior responders.

**3. Postmortem Without Alert Cleanup**: Teams write thorough 5-page postmortems on the root cause while leaving the 40 noisy alerts that masked the real signal untouched.

## Measuring & sustaining healthy on-call rotations

Track operational health metrics for your on-call program just like service SLOs:

- **Target Toil Budget**: <= 2 off-hours pages per 7-day shift per engineer. Any alert firing >2x/week without a code/config fix is auto-reviewed.
- **GameDays**: Run quarterly Chaos/GameDay drills during business hours (e.g., terminating a primary AZ or injecting DNS failure) to verify escalation paths, runbook accuracy, and IC handoffs before a real 2 AM outage.
- **Compensatory Time Off**: Provide automatic recovery time after disruptive overnight SEV-1 responses to prevent cumulative burnout.

## Practical checklist

- [ ] Maintain at least 6–8 engineers per 24/7 rotation (or use follow-the-sun regional handoffs).
- [ ] Configure 5-minute L1 -> L2 -> L3 escalation timeouts with push, SMS, and voice fallback.
- [ ] Require `runbook_url`, severity, and owning team metadata on 100% of paging alerts.
- [ ] Separate Incident Commander (coordination) from SMEs (mitigation) on all SEV-1/SEV-2 events.
- [ ] Run an external dead-man's-switch heartbeat monitor to detect broken alerting pipelines.
- [ ] Review page volume weekly and delete or fix any non-actionable alert within 48 hours.

interviewProblems.title: On-Call Escalation Policies
interviewProblems.scenarioPrompt: Design a production system that depends on On-Call Escalation Policies. What invariants, failure modes, and observability do you require?
interviewProblems.sampleDefense: Start from invariants, choose the pattern that preserves them, and add metrics for the known failure modes.
commonPitfalls: Optimizing throughput before defining correctness boundaries.

steps.title: 1. Normal Request Ingress
steps.explanation: On-call escalation defines deterministic routing, acknowledgment SLAs, and tiered handoffs so production incidents reach the right responder fast without burning out engineers. Effective escalation pairs automated multi-channel paging (PagerDuty/Opsgenie) with explicit severity tiers, Incident Commander (IC) roles, and blameless post-incident feedback loops.

steps.title: 2. Core Execution & State Lookup
steps.explanation: Level 2: Secondary / SME applies the primary invariant and coordinates with SEV-1 Incident Commander.

steps.title: 3. Scale Spike / Failure Injection
steps.explanation: Under a 10x burst, SEV-1 Incident Commander experiences contention and tail-latency amplification.

steps.title: 4. Mitigation & Steady Recovery
steps.explanation: Delete or downgrade any alert that doesn't require immediate human action; require every page to link to a tested runbook.

tipsAndTricks: Core mental model: Keep Tier-1 pages strictly actionable with a 5-minute acknowledgment timeout before escalating to a secondary, separate the Incident Commander from hands-on debuggers on SEV-1/SEV-2, and enforce a 48-hour SLA to fix or delete any noisy alert.
Avoid trap: Creating alerts without a `runbook_url`—forcing a half-asleep engineer at 3 AM to read source code to figure out what a metric means.
Avoid trap: Routing pages solely to Slack or email instead of phone/SMS/high-priority push notifications that bypass Do Not Disturb.
When to reach for it: Operating 24/7 production services with explicit availability SLOs (99.9%+) where delayed human intervention violates customer SLAs.
When to reach for it: Scaling beyond a single 6-person team into multi-team microservice ownership where incidents cross network, database, and application boundaries.

putItTogether.title: Putting On Call Escalation Together
putItTogether.summary: Keep Tier-1 pages strictly actionable with a 5-minute acknowledgment timeout before escalating to a secondary, separate the Incident Commander from hands-on debuggers on SEV-1/SEV-2, and enforce a 48-hour SLA to fix or delete any noisy alert.
steps: Establish baseline invariants for On Call Escalation before scaling.
Isolate hot paths with caching, backpressure, or partitioning.
Verify failure modes with synthetic load & chaos checks.
putItTogether.outcome: Migrating critical SLO burn alerts to PagerDuty with a 5-minute push-to-phone-call escalation and automatic fallback to the Secondary + Platform Lead cut MTTA to 2.8 minutes and eliminated missed pages.
